title: Secrets Management: Stores, Rotation and Injection
objectives: Describe what a secrets manager adds beyond encrypted variables
Choose between environment variables, mounted files and fetched secrets for a workload
Plan a rotation that never drops live traffic

cards.title: What makes a secret different from configuration
cards.body: A secret is configuration whose value must stay confidential: a database password, an API key, a signing key. That changes the requirements. Alongside delivery it needs access scoped by identity, a log of every read and a plan for replacing the value while the service keeps running.

cards.title: A secrets manager in the middle
cards.body: A secrets manager stores values centrally, checks the caller’s identity against policy, audits every read and can rotate on a schedule. Some also mint dynamic secrets: a database user created for one workload with a TTL, deleted automatically when it expires.

cards.title: Worked example: rotating a shared API key
cards.body: A key used by twenty services must be replaced without an outage.
steps: Issue a second key while the first keeps working
Roll the new key out to the services over a normal deploy
Watch usage until calls authenticated with the old key stop
Revoke the old key; the overlap is what made it safe

cards.title: Environment variables versus mounted files
cards.body: An environment variable is fixed when the process starts: a rotated value cannot reach a running process without a restart, and variables leak into crash dumps and child processes. A mounted file can be refreshed by the platform and re-read by the app, at the cost of the app knowing to look again.

cards.title: Misconception: encrypted at rest means safe
cards.body: Encrypting a secret and committing it is not access control: everyone holding the key, now or later through git history, holds every version. Encryption answers at-rest exposure; it does nothing about who may decrypt, when the value should change or what happens after a leak.

cards.title: Trap: secrets that live forever in CI settings
cards.body: A permanent token pasted into pipeline variables outlives the project, the person who created it and every fork of the job. When it leaks, through a log, a misconfigured job or a departed engineer, nobody knows what it could reach. Prefer credentials the job mints from its own workload identity, valid for minutes.

questions.prompt: Why keep production secrets in a central secrets manager rather than in each CI system’s variables?

choices.label: It encrypts secrets other stores cannot encrypt
One place scopes access, logs reads and rotates values
Workloads then need no credentials of their own
Developers can read the values more quickly

questions.explanation: The gains are operational, not cryptographic: CI variables are encrypted too, but a central store gives one policy surface, one audit log and one rotation point. Workloads still authenticate, and ease of reading is the opposite of the goal.

questions.prompt: Why deliver a frequently rotated password as a mounted file rather than an environment variable?

choices.label: Files hide the value from anyone on the host
Environment variables cannot hold long secrets
Mounted files are encrypted on disk by default
The app can re-read the new value without restarting

questions.explanation: An environment variable is fixed at process start, so a rotation needs a restart to propagate; a file the platform refreshes lets the app pick up the new value in place. Files are not inherently hidden or encrypted, and variables hold any length.

questions.prompt: A deploy log prints a live API key. The team enables log masking. What still must happen?

choices.label: Re-run the deploy so the key is used correctly
Nothing: masking removes it from the log history
Rotate the key: masking does not change the value
Purge the stored logs so the key cannot be re-read

questions.explanation: Masking changes what future log output shows, not the credential itself; anyone who saw the log keeps a working key until it is rotated. Deleting logs helps but is not guaranteed, and re-running the deploy does nothing for the leaked value.

questions.prompt: A platform team rotates 240 secrets by hand each quarter at about 25 minutes each. How many engineer-hours is that per quarter?
assumptions: 240 secrets, one manual rotation each per quarter
25 minutes of engineer time per rotation (illustrative)
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 25 minutes is a little under half an hour, so the total should land just under 120 hours. Automation that cuts each rotation to a 5-minute review saves about 80 hours every quarter.

questions.prompt: Order a zero-downtime rotation of a shared API key.

items.label: Watch until calls on the old key stop
Issue a second key while the first still works
Revoke the old key
Roll the new key out to every caller

questions.explanation: The overlap is the whole trick: two valid keys let callers migrate on a normal deploy. Revoking before usage stops just moves the outage to a different clock, and issuing only one key forces a coordinated cutover.

questions.prompt: A nightly batch job needs to read from a cloud database.
constraints: Job runs once a day for an hour
A stored password would sit valid for months
Every workload already has a platform identity

approaches.label: A stored password, rotated by hand each quarter
One shared admin password kept in the team vault
The job exchanges its workload identity for a short-lived credential each run

rationaleOptions.label: A quarterly rotation is often enough for a leaked key
A credential that lives an hour bounds what a leak can do
A shared password is safe while few people know it
There is no long-lived value to store or rotate

rationaleConflicts.r3: Months of validity is exactly the exposure rotation exists to shrink.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Shared credentials make audit trails and revocation painful.

questions.explanation: The job already owns an identity, so it can mint a credential that exists for the run and is gone after; a leaked value then expires before anyone uses it. A quarterly password spends most of its life waiting to leak, and a shared admin credential can reach far more than the job needs.

flashcards.back: Static lives until rotated; dynamic is minted per use with a TTL and dies on its own.
To bound how long a leaked value stays useful.

flashcards.front: Env var vs mounted file for a rotating secret?
flashcards.back: The file can be refreshed and re-read; the variable is fixed for the life of the process.

mechanism.title: How a workload actually gets a secret
steps: The workload starts with an identity it already owns: a service account token, an instance identity or a signed CI job token. No secret is needed to prove who it is, which is what breaks the bootstrap problem.
The secrets broker checks that identity against its trust configuration: which issuer it accepts, which subject and audience the token must carry and which workload it maps to.
A policy then decides which paths or roles that identity may read, ideally as narrowly as the workload’s real need. Broad policies quietly recreate the shared-password problem inside the manager.
The store either returns a stored value or generates a dynamic credential, such as a database user created on the spot with a TTL and scheduled deletion, so nothing permanent exists to steal.

Delivery is the last hop: the value lands in a mounted file the platform can refresh, or in memory the app fetched itself. Either way it never sits in source control, image layers or pipeline variables.
On rotation or expiry the new credential is already working before the old one is revoked, and the app re-reads the file or re-fetches. Rotation becomes routine rather than a maintenance window.

useWhen: Use a central secrets store whenever more than one system needs the same credentials.
Prefer dynamic, TTL-bound credentials for databases and cloud APIs that support them.
Rotate on suspicion, not only on schedule.
avoidWhen: Do not bake secrets into images, build artefacts or source control, even encrypted ones if the key is widely held.
Avoid environment variables for secrets that rotate; the process keeps the old value until restarted.
Do not let every workload read every secret; broad policies undo the point of the store.

rows: Fixed at process start; leaks into dumps and subprocesses
Refreshes without a restart; stays out of the environment
App must re-read it; file permissions need care
Tight audit trail; rotation logic lives in the app
Couples the app to the store; fetch failures need handling
Sidecar or agent syncs to files
App reads plain files; platform handles renewal
One more component to run and secure

numbers.title: What hand rotation costs as secrets multiply
assumptions: 240 secrets rotated quarterly (illustrative)
25 minutes per manual rotation versus 5 minutes of review for an automated one
steps: Manual: 240 × 25 minutes = 6,000 minutes = 100 hours a quarter, about 2.5 weeks of one engineer’s time.
Automated: 240 × 5 minutes = 1,200 minutes = 20 hours a quarter.
The 80-hour difference recurs every quarter and grows with every new service and credential.
Manual rotation also tends to slip, so secrets live longer than policy intends.
numbers.result: Rotation that is cheap happens on time; rotation that is toil happens late or never.

india.title: What the public guidance says
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet recommends centralising secrets in a dedicated manager, scoping access by identity, auditing every read and preferring short-lived dynamic credentials over long-lived static ones. Vendor documentation follows the same shape: cloud secrets managers pair stored secrets with automatic rotation, and workload-identity federation lets a job mint temporary credentials instead of holding a permanent key in CI settings.

pitfalls.trap: “We mask secrets in the logs, so a leak is handled.”
pitfalls.say: “Masking stops the next print; the value that already leaked stays valid until I rotate it.”

pitfalls.trap: “The secret is encrypted in the repository, so it is safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Encrypted at rest is not access control; anyone with the key or the decrypt job gets every version in the history.”

takeaways: Secrets need identity-scoped access, audit and rotation; config does not.
Prefer short-lived credentials minted from workload identity.
Deliver by file or fetch so rotation does not force a restart.
Masking logs is hygiene, not remediation; rotate after any leak.

interactive.title: The masked leak
interactive.prompt: A deploy job prints a live API key into CI logs. The team turns on secret masking, deletes nothing else and moves on. A month later, what is true of the leaked key?

choices.label: It can still be used by anyone who saw the log, until it is rotated
choices.feedback: Right: masking changes what future logs show, not the credential.

choices.label: It stopped working when masking was enabled
choices.feedback: Masking edits log output, not the key itself.

choices.label: It expired on its own shortly after the log was written
choices.feedback: Static secrets have no expiry; they live until rotated or revoked.

interactive.reveal: After any leak the remediation is rotation plus a look at who could read the log. Masking and log access control shrink the audience; they do not heal the credential.

seeAlso.why: Least privilege and defence in depth, applied to credentials
Workload identity is what lets a job mint credentials instead of storing them
Pipelines are where secrets most often leak into logs and artefacts

title: Supply-Chain Security for Containers: SBOMs, Scanning and Signing
objectives: Explain what an image scan does and does not tell you
Describe how SBOMs, signatures and admission checks tie a running pod back to a trusted build
Choose gating rules that keep findings actionable rather than ignored

cards.title: Every dependency is somebody else’s code
cards.body: A production image holds a base operating system, runtime packages and application dependencies, all chosen by other people and all carrying their vulnerabilities. You ship whatever they shipped, so you need to know what is in the box and how you will hear when part of it goes bad.

cards.title: Scanning reports what you shipped
cards.body: A scanner indexes the packages inside an image and matches them against a vulnerability feed, reporting findings with severity and often a fixed version. Two consequences follow: the base image sets your noise floor, and a scan is a snapshot, true only until the feed moves.

cards.title: An SBOM is the ingredients list
cards.body: A software bill of materials records every package and version inside an image, generated at build and stored next to it. On disclosure day it turns “are we affected?” from an audit of every running system into a single query.

cards.title: Signing and admission bind runtime to pipeline
cards.body: The pipeline signs the image digest with its own identity and records provenance: which source and build produced it. An admission check in the cluster verifies the signature before a pod may start, so an image that bypassed the pipeline cannot run.

cards.title: Worked example: answering a same-day vulnerability
cards.body: A critical CVE is published in a common compression library at noon.
steps: Query the SBOM index for every deployed image containing the library
The result: 24 of 400 images carry it, listed by digest
Rebuild those images from a patched base in the normal pipeline
Redeploy by digest; the admission check confirms each new signature

cards.title: Trap: scanning only at build time
cards.body: A clean scan at build is true for one afternoon. Vulnerabilities are published daily into code that has not changed in months, so an image grows worse sitting in the registry. Continuous rescanning of stored and running images is what keeps the statement “we are clean” honest.

questions.prompt: What does a kept SBOM let a team answer in minutes?

choices.label: Whether a container is running as root
How much each image costs to store
Which deployed images contain a newly disclosed package
Which images sit in the wrong region

questions.explanation: The SBOM is the package index per image, so a new disclosure becomes a lookup over what is deployed. Privilege, cost and placement are properties of the runtime and the registry, not of the ingredients list.

questions.prompt: A cluster verifies the signature on an image digest before admitting a pod. What does a valid signature prove?

choices.label: This exact image content came from the trusted pipeline
The image contains no known vulnerabilities
The image was built from a minimal base
The registry holds an uncorrupted copy

questions.explanation: The signature binds the digest, which is the content, to the signer’s identity: provenance. It says nothing about what is inside, so a signed image can still be vulnerable, built from a fat base or mirrored faithfully.

questions.prompt: An image that scanned clean at build fails the nightly rescan two months later. What changed?

choices.label: The image quietly mutated inside the registry
The scanner lost access to the package index
The base image tag moved to a newer build
A vulnerability in a packaged dependency was published since

questions.explanation: The image is unchanged; the feed moved. A finding on an old, unmodified image almost always means a new CVE was published against code it has carried all along, which is exactly why rescanning exists.

questions.prompt: Order the checks a supply-chain-hardened release passes through.

items.label: Generate the SBOM and scan the image
Deploy by digest so pods run
Build the image from a pinned base
Admission verifies signature and policy
Sign the digest and record provenance

questions.explanation: Each later check depends on the earlier artefact: you cannot scan or sign an image that does not exist, and the signature is only meaningful because admission verifies it before the workload is allowed to start.

questions.prompt: An estate runs 400 deployed images. An SBOM query finds a vulnerable library in 6% of them. How many images need a rebuild?
assumptions: 400 distinct deployed images
6% carry the library (illustrative)
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 6% is a little under one sixteenth, and 400 ÷ 16 = 25, so the answer belongs in the mid-twenties. Without the index the team would be auditing all 400 by hand.

questions.prompt: Security wants no image with a critical, fixable vulnerability running in production.
constraints: Scans flag hundreds of low-risk findings

approaches.label: Block a deploy on any finding, whatever its severity
Block deploys on critical findings and rescan running images continuously
Run one fleet-wide vulnerability scan each quarter

rationaleOptions.label: Rescanning catches CVEs published after the build
Quarterly scans reach disclosures soon enough
A severity gate keeps the deploy path usable
Blocking every finding stays cheap when scans are noisy

rationaleConflicts.r3: A gate that floods gets bypassed or ignored, which is worse than a risk-based one.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Daily disclosures make a quarterly scan a months-long exposure window.

questions.explanation: Gating on criticals keeps the deploy path fast enough that teams respect it, while continuous rescanning closes the gap between a CVE being published and the vulnerable image being noticed. Blocking everything trains workarounds, and quarterly scanning leaves weeks of silent exposure.

flashcards.back: The ingredients list of an image: every package and version, produced at build.

flashcards.front: What does a signature on a digest prove?
flashcards.back: That exact content came from the signer; nothing about vulnerabilities.
New CVEs are published daily; a clean build ages into a vulnerable one.

sources.title: SLSA: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts
Docker Docs: Image build best practices

mechanism.title: From commit to admitted pod
steps: The build starts from a pinned, minimal base. Fewer packages mean a shorter ingredients list, a smaller attack surface and a lower noise floor on every future scan.
The SBOM generator walks the build context and layers and records every package and version; the list is stored beside the image so later queries need no access to running systems.
The scanner matches that index against a vulnerability feed and reports findings with severity and fix availability; the same matching runs again whenever the feed updates, which is daily.
The pipeline signs the image digest with its own workload identity and attaches provenance: which source, which build and which steps produced the artefact.
The registry keeps image, SBOM, scan report and attestations together. Deploying by digest guarantees the artefact that was checked is the one that runs.
In the cluster an admission controller verifies the signature and policy before a pod may start, so an image that skipped the pipeline cannot begin.
Between deploys, rescanning watches the feed; when a new CVE lands in a running image, the SBOM index turns the response into a rebuild list rather than an estate-wide audit.

useWhen: Sign and verify for any cluster that runs third-party or multi-team images.
Keep SBOMs for every deployed image so disclosure days are lookups, not audits.
Rescan continuously; the feed moves even when nothing deploys.
avoidWhen: Do not gate on every finding; a gate that floods gets bypassed.
Avoid scanning only at build time; it is a point-in-time answer.
Do not treat signing as a vulnerability check; provenance and hygiene answer different questions.

rows: Short SBOM, few findings, small attack surface
No shell or tools; debugging takes extra steps
Longer SBOM; more findings to triage
Deploys keep moving; new CVEs still surface
Some accepted risk below the gate
Noise drowns the gate; teams route around it

numbers.title: Disclosure day, with and without an index
assumptions: 400 deployed images; a critical CVE lands in a common library (illustrative)
A manual audit costs 20 minutes per service; an indexed query is instant
steps: Manual audit: 400 × 20 minutes ≈ 133 engineer-hours, spread over days while the vulnerability stays open.
Indexed query: the 6% of images carrying the package surface immediately, 24 rebuilds instead of 400 checks.
Each rebuild from a patched base takes about 15 minutes of pipeline time, roughly 6 hours of compute that can run in parallel.
The exposure window shrinks from days of auditing to the time it takes to rebuild and roll.
numbers.result: An SBOM index turns disclosure response from a per-service audit into a rebuild list.

india.title: The SLSA supply-chain framework
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The SLSA framework, published at slsa.dev, describes supply-chain integrity in levels: provenance recording how an artefact was built, isolated build systems and signed attestations that consumers verify before use. Kubernetes documentation likewise covers admission-time verification of signed images, so a cluster only runs images a trusted pipeline produced. Together these are the mechanisms a container supply-chain control is built from.

pitfalls.trap: “The image was scanned, so it is clean.”
pitfalls.say: “It was clean against that feed on that day; rescanning is what keeps the statement true.”

pitfalls.trap: “The dependency was bumped, so the vulnerability is fixed.”
pitfalls.say: “Only once a new image is built from it, redeployed by digest and the old one stopped.”

takeaways: Scan results expire; rescan as the feed moves.
SBOMs make “are we affected?” a query, not an audit.
Sign digests and verify at admission to bind runtime to pipeline.
Minimal bases shrink both attack surface and finding noise.

interactive.title: The lunchtime CVE
interactive.prompt: At noon a critical vulnerability is published in a library baked into many images. Which team can say within the hour whether it is affected?

choices.label: The team keeping an SBOM index for every deployed image
choices.feedback: Right: one query over package names produces the rebuild list.

choices.label: The team that scans every image at build time
choices.feedback: Their scan reports are as old as each build; nothing re-runs on a new CVE.

choices.label: The team whose clusters verify image signatures
choices.feedback: Signatures prove where an image came from, not what is inside it.

interactive.reveal: SBOMs answer “where is this package?”; scanning answers “is it vulnerable?”; signing answers “did our pipeline make it?”. Disclosure day needs the first one.

seeAlso.why: How the containers being secured actually run in production
Layers, digests and multi-stage builds are what SBOMs and scans operate on
Admission control is where signature verification is enforced

title: Observability Signals: Metrics, Logs, Traces and Cardinality
objectives: Pick the signal that answers an operational question cheapest
Explain how cardinality turns one label into a storage bill
Describe how trace context travels across services

cards.title: Three signals answer different questions
cards.body: Metrics are cheap aggregates over time: is it bad, and since when? Logs are events with full context: what exactly happened here? Traces follow one request across services: where did the time go? Asking the wrong signal is how teams end up drowning in data and starved of answers.

cards.title: Cardinality is the meter on the metrics bill
cards.body: Every distinct combination of label values is its own stored time series. A status label with three values triples one metric; a user id label with two million values turns it into two million series. Storage, memory and query time all scale with series count.

cards.title: Worked example: one request, one trace
cards.body: A checkout request crosses six services and one is slow.
steps: The edge service creates a trace id and a root span
Each hop adds a child span carrying the same trace id
Sampling keeps all errors and a fraction of routine traffic
The waterfall shows the inventory service holding 800 of the 900 ms

cards.title: Sampling keeps traces affordable
cards.body: Recording every span at high request rates is expensive and mostly boring. Head sampling decides early and cheap; tail sampling decides after the request finished, so it can keep every error and slow outlier while storing only a sliver of routine work.

cards.title: Misconception: more telemetry always means more insight
cards.body: Unbounded cardinality, full-fidelity logs and 100% trace sampling all raise cost faster than they raise understanding. Instrument to answer the questions you actually ask: symptom alerts, per-hop diagnosis and post-incident detail.

cards.title: Trap: logging what should never be stored
cards.body: Logs are the easiest place to accidentally build a data breach: request bodies, tokens and personal data flow straight into a system built for searching, not secrecy. Redact fields at emission, and treat log access as sensitive access.

questions.prompt: Which signal most cheaply answers “is fleet-wide p99 latency rising?”

choices.label: Full request logs from every service
Aggregated metrics per service
A stored trace of every request
Weekly error summary reports

questions.explanation: A latency histogram per service costs a handful of series and answers the question continuously. Logs and full tracing record per request, orders of magnitude more data than a fleet-wide symptom needs.

questions.prompt: A team adds customer id as a label on a request metric across 2,000,000 customers. What happens?

choices.label: Queries speed up because data is pre-grouped
Nothing until the metric is actually queried
The metric is sampled down to a fixed size
A series per customer: storage and query cost explode

questions.explanation: Each distinct label value set is a series the system must store, index and scan. Two million values means two million series for one metric, where drill-down by customer is what traces and logs exist for.

questions.prompt: Why does a tracing system inject a trace id into outbound request headers?

choices.label: So spans from different services join into one trace
So downstream services can rate-limit the caller
So the request can be deduplicated on retries
So trace data is encrypted end to end

questions.explanation: Context propagation is what lets a span recorded in service C be placed under the span from service B. Without the id in the header, each service produces orphan fragments that no collector can stitch together.

questions.prompt: A metric carries two labels: status (3 values) and endpoint (200 values). Across 50 pods, how many series does that pair create?
assumptions: Every label value combination on every pod is a distinct series
Labels are independent, so counts multiply
questions.explanation: Sanity check: each pod holds 3 × 200 = 600 series, so 50 pods must land in the tens of thousands. Swap endpoint for user id and the same multiplication explains a blown metrics budget.

questions.prompt: Order a trace-guided hunt for a slow request.

items.label: Open that service’s logs around the span
Watch the latency metric rise
Find the span holding most of the time
Pull traces of the slowest requests

questions.explanation: Metrics say that it is slow, traces say where, logs say why. Each signal narrows the search before the more expensive one is opened, which is why the signals are used as a funnel rather than interchangeably.

questions.prompt: Checkout latency doubled and forty services sit on the request path.

approaches.label: Full-fidelity logs of every request at every hop
Fleet metrics for health, plus traces sampled with all errors kept
Metrics only; skip tracing to save money

rationaleOptions.label: Full logs at forty hops stay cheap under a cap
Metrics find the spike cheaply; traces name the hop
Metrics alone can show which hop is guilty
Keeping all error traces costs little volume

rationaleConflicts.r3: Forty services logging every request in full is exactly the spend the cap forbids.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A per-service metric says that hop is slow only after the slow service is known to matter; the trace is what points at it first.

questions.explanation: Metrics localise the symptom cheaply, and sampled traces identify which of the forty hops holds the time, with error traces always kept since they are the interesting minority. Logging everything blows the cap; metrics alone stall at knowing something, somewhere, is slow.

flashcards.back: Metric: fleet health over time. Log: one event in detail. Trace: one request’s path across services.
The number of distinct label value combinations on a metric; each is a stored series.
Head decides at request start; tail decides after, so it can keep all errors and outliers.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How one request becomes one trace
steps: At the edge, the first service creates a trace id and a root span, then propagates the id in headers on every call it makes downstream.
Each service starts a child span on arrival and ends it on reply, recording duration, status and a few low-cardinality attributes such as route and result.
Propagation is the load-bearing step: without the id in the header, downstream spans become orphan fragments that cannot be stitched into the request’s story.
Agents or a collector receive spans, batch them and apply sampling policy: routine traffic sampled down, errors and slow outliers kept whole.
Metrics run a separate, cheaper pipeline: counters and histograms aggregate as they are recorded, so fleet health costs a few series per service rather than a record per request.
Logs carry the detail that fits neither: they are the most expensive per byte, so they earn their keep on errors and unusual paths, structured so a trace id can pivot straight to them.
Cardinality is the hidden multiplier in metrics: every distinct label value set becomes its own series, so one unbounded label can cost more than every other metric combined.

useWhen: Metrics for dashboards, alerts and SLOs; the cheapest signal per question.
Traces where a request crosses many services and the guilty hop is unknown.
Structured logs with trace ids for detail after the trace has pointed.
avoidWhen: Never put unbounded values (user id, session id, full path) into metric labels.
Do not keep every span at high request rates; sample and keep all errors.
Avoid logging payloads wholesale; cost and leaked data grow together.

rows: Expensive at volume; easy to over-collect

numbers.title: How one label becomes a storage bill
assumptions: 200 metrics per pod, 100 pods (illustrative)
Each label multiplies series by its number of distinct values
steps: Base: 200 × 100 = 20,000 series, already the cost floor.
Add a 3-value status label to one metric: it triples, a modest bump.
Add user id with 500,000 values to that metric: it alone becomes 500,000 series, twenty-five times the entire base.
Query latency and memory track series count, so the dashboard slows before anyone sees the invoice.
numbers.result: Cardinality is a multiplier, not an add-on; bound a label’s values or leave it out of metrics.

india.title: What OpenTelemetry standardises
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: OpenTelemetry’s documentation defines the three signals, traces, metrics and logs, and standardises context propagation so a trace id survives across services and vendors. Google’s SRE book describes monitoring through the golden signals, latency, traffic, errors and saturation, all of which are metric-shaped questions. The division of labour is deliberate: metrics answer fleet questions cheaply, traces follow single requests and logs hold the detail.

pitfalls.trap: “Add request id as a label so we can drill down.”
pitfalls.say: “That is a series per request; drill-down is what trace ids and logs are for.”

pitfalls.trap: “Sample 1% of all spans to save money.”
pitfalls.say: “Sample the boring 99%; keep every error and outlier, or the traces that mattered are gone.”

takeaways: Metrics for is-it-bad, traces for where, logs for why.
Cardinality multiplies cost; bound every label’s values.
Propagate trace context or traces split at the hop boundary.
Sample aggressively but keep all errors.

interactive.title: One more label
interactive.prompt: A service adds plan_tier (3 values) to a metric; fine. Next sprint someone adds session_id. A week later the metrics backend is slow and the bill has jumped. What happened?

choices.label: Every session minted new series, and series are the unit of cost
choices.feedback: Right: unbounded label values multiply the series count without limit.

choices.label: Sessions ran long, so each series accumulated too many points
choices.feedback: Extra points cost little; the count of distinct series is what hurts.

choices.label: The backend charges per label name on a metric
choices.feedback: It is the distinct value combinations, not the label itself, that create series.

interactive.reveal: Label values must have a bound you can say out loud. If you cannot bound it, it belongs in a trace attribute or a log field, not a metric label.

seeAlso.why: The same three signals from the system-design side
SLIs are built from these signals
Alerts page on the symptoms these signals surface

title: Capacity Planning and Headroom
objectives: Explain what headroom buys and what it costs
Turn a demand forecast into a replica or capacity count
Name the lead times that make capacity a planning problem

cards.title: Headroom is bought before you need it
cards.body: Some capacity arrives in seconds and some in weeks. Pods start fast; nodes take minutes; quota raises, reserved contracts and new regions take days. A capacity plan exists because the lead times do not match, and the slow items must be handled before the peak, not during it.

cards.title: Utilisation targets buy reaction time
cards.body: A 60% utilisation target is not waste; it is the room where bursts, deploys and one lost node can land. As utilisation approaches saturation, queueing delay climbs steeply, so the same service that is cheap at 95% is also one jittery afternoon from meltdown.

cards.title: Worked example: from forecast to replica count
cards.body: Next quarter’s peak is forecast at 5,000 requests a second.
steps: Load testing says a replica serves 250 rps at the 60% utilisation target
5,000 ÷ 250 = 20 working replicas
Add 20% headroom for failure and deploy overlap: 24 replicas
Check the quota and subnet allow 24 before the quarter starts

cards.title: Forecast demand from business drivers
cards.body: The demand side is not a graph extrapolation alone: it is growth trends plus the events calendar. Launches, marketing pushes and seasonal peaks all move the peak, and honest plans are ranges with dates, revisited each quarter rather than a single number computed once.

cards.title: Misconception: autoscaling removes the need to plan
cards.body: Autoscaling spends provisioned headroom inside limits someone set: cluster size, quotas, warm pools and budget. It handles the shape of a normal day beautifully; it cannot create a node the quota forbids or a contract nobody signed.

cards.title: Trap: planning to one hundred per cent
cards.body: A plan that only works at 100% utilisation leaves nowhere for a rolling deploy’s extra pods, a zone event or arrival jitter to go. Sizing to the average is the quieter version of the same mistake: the peak is what breaks you, so the peak is what you provision for.

questions.prompt: Why run a latency-sensitive service at a 60% utilisation target rather than 95%?

choices.label: Providers bill less below 70% utilisation
Monitoring is more accurate below two thirds
Bursts, deploys and failures need spare capacity to land in
Each instance runs measurably faster when less loaded

questions.explanation: The spare 40% is reaction time made physical: it absorbs spikes before autoscaling reacts, extra pods during deploys and the loss of a node. Near saturation, queueing delay climbs steeply, so the saved fleet cost is traded for fragility.

questions.prompt: Which lead time must a capacity plan handle ahead of a launch?

choices.label: A provider quota raise that can take days
A container restart that takes seconds
A DNS record that propagates in a minute
A configuration rollout that takes an hour

questions.explanation: Quotas, reserved contracts and new-region approvals are the slow items, measured in days, so they belong in a plan made before the peak. Restarts, DNS and config changes all fit inside the window where the launch is already happening.

questions.prompt: Average CPU is 35%, but every weekday at 6 p.m. the service saturates for ten minutes. What should the plan size to?

choices.label: The daily average, since peaks are brief
The busiest second ever recorded
Whatever the autoscaler last requested
The recurring peak plus headroom

questions.explanation: Users experience the peak, not the average; a service sized to 35% melts at 6 p.m. daily. The single highest second is noise rather than a target, and last request is a measurement, not a forecast.

questions.prompt: Forecast peak is 5,000 requests a second. A replica serves 250 at the utilisation target, and the plan reserves 20% for failures. How many replicas should be provisioned?
assumptions: Demand divides evenly across replicas
The 20% reserve sits on top of the working count
questions.explanation: Design implication: 20 replicas carry the forecast only while nothing fails; the 4 extra are the margin that absorbs a lost node or a rolling deploy without turning it into a capacity emergency.

questions.prompt: Order a quarterly capacity review.

items.label: Revisit the plan and re-measure the ratio
Convert demand into per-resource needs
Provision ahead of the peak
Gather growth trends and planned events
Check quotas, budgets and lead times

questions.explanation: Forecast first, translate to resources, then clear the slow constraints before provisioning; the review closes the loop by re-measuring the demand-per-replica ratio that the whole plan rests on.

questions.prompt: A retail service sees 4× normal traffic on one festival weekend a year.
constraints: Extra nodes need a week’s notice
Running 4× all year quadruples the bill

approaches.label: Let autoscaling find the capacity on the day
Pre-provision for the known peak, then release the capacity
Run 4× capacity all year to stay safe

rationaleOptions.label: The peak is on the calendar, so it can be provisioned ahead
Year-round 4× is cheap insurance
Autoscaling can fetch any amount of capacity quickly
Lead time, not reaction speed, is the constraint

rationaleConflicts.r3: A week of procurement cannot be compressed into minutes on the day.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It quadruples cost to cover two days of need.

questions.explanation: A known peak is a scheduling problem, not a scaling problem: provision before the window, ride it, release after. Autoscaling cannot beat the week-long lead time, and permanent 4× capacity pays all year for a weekend.

flashcards.back: Provisioned spare capacity that absorbs bursts, deploys and failures.
Nowhere for jitter, deploys or a lost node to go; queues explode near saturation.
Quota raises, reserved contracts and new regions take days; pods take seconds.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Software Engineering in SRE

mechanism.title: How a capacity plan is built
steps: Start from demand, not machines: forecast the peak in business terms, orders per minute or requests per second, from growth trends and the events calendar.
Convert demand to resources with a tested ratio: if a replica serves 250 rps at the utilisation target, a 5,000 rps forecast means twenty working replicas before any margin.
Add failure headroom: the count must still serve the peak while a node, a rack or a zone is missing, which is why targets sit near 60% rather than 95%.
Add change headroom: rolling deploys and autoscaler churn run extra copies at once, so the cluster needs room for the old and new versions together.
Check the constraints: provider quotas, subnet addresses, licence limits and budget all cap the plan, and each has a lead time measured in days rather than seconds.
Provision ahead and rehearse: quotas are raised and limits bumped before the peak, then a load test confirms the forecast ratio still holds on current code.
Review on a cadence: growth compounds quietly, so the plan is revisited each quarter and the ratio re-measured whenever the service changes shape.

useWhen: Forecast and pre-provision for known peaks: launches, festivals, sales.
Keep utilisation targets that leave room for failures plus deploy overlap.
Re-measure the demand-per-replica ratio after large code changes.
avoidWhen: Do not size to the daily average; peaks and failures are what break services.
Do not assume autoscaling creates capacity; it only spends provisioned headroom.
Avoid single-point forecasts; plan ranges and revisit them.

rows: No room for bursts; queues explode
Cannot beat quotas or warm-up time
Needs forecasting; pays for the window

numbers.title: When to order the next tranche
assumptions: Traffic grows 8% a month from 2,000 rps today (illustrative)
Provisioned capacity is 4,000 rps and new capacity takes 6 weeks to arrive
steps: At 8% monthly growth demand doubles in about nine months: 2,000 × 1.08^9 ≈ 4,000 rps.
Existing headroom therefore runs out in roughly nine months.
A 6-week lead time means the order lands around month seven, not when the dashboard turns red.
Early ordering also covers forecast error: at 10% growth the headroom is gone in about seven months.
numbers.result: Capacity planning is mostly calendar arithmetic: work backwards from the lead time.

india.title: The Tatkal opening spike
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: India’s railway booking platform sees demand concentrate at fixed times each day: the Tatkal window opens at 10:00 for AC classes and 11:00 for non-AC, and publicly reported figures describe large shares of each day’s Tatkal tickets selling within minutes of the window opening. It is a textbook known peak: the spike sits in the calendar, so the capacity for it has to be provisioned ahead rather than discovered on the day.

pitfalls.trap: “We autoscale, so capacity planning is done for us.”
pitfalls.say: “Autoscaling spends headroom inside limits I set; the limits, quotas and warm pools are still planned.”

pitfalls.trap: “Buy for the worst imaginable day and forget it.”
pitfalls.say: “Idle forever-capacity is a bill; I would rather plan ranges with lead times than a permanent peak.”

takeaways: Plan for peak plus failures, not the average day.
Utilisation targets are bought reaction time.
Quotas, contracts and provisioning all carry lead times.
Autoscaling spends headroom; it does not create it.

interactive.title: Quota day
interactive.prompt: A festival weekend needs 4× capacity. The team trusts autoscaling; the node quota allows 3× and quota raises take a week. On the day, traffic hits 3.5×. What do users see?

choices.label: Growing queues and errors: scaling stops at the quota wall
choices.feedback: Right: the autoscaler keeps requesting nodes the quota refuses to grant.

choices.label: Nothing unusual: autoscaling adds nodes until demand is met
choices.feedback: The quota is the ceiling; requests above it are simply denied.

choices.label: A few seconds of slowness while the new nodes boot
choices.feedback: Boot time is not the constraint; the missing quarter of capacity never arrives.

interactive.reveal: Lead-time items, quotas, reserved capacity and contracts, belong in a capacity plan reviewed before the peak, because they cannot be fixed during it.

seeAlso.why: Failure headroom is what lets a service lose a zone or region and keep serving
Autoscaling consumes the headroom this plan provides
The demand-per-replica ratio comes from load testing

title: Kubernetes DNS and Service Discovery
objectives: Describe how a pod turns a Service name into a connection
Explain when a headless Service is the right answer
Diagnose common DNS failure modes: search expansion, missing endpoints and overload

cards.title: A name per Service, not per pod
cards.body: Cluster DNS publishes records like payments.shop.svc.cluster.local that map to a stable virtual IP, while pods come and go underneath it. Callers name a Service, never a pod, and the name survives every rollout.

cards.title: CoreDNS answers for the whole cluster
cards.body: A small set of DNS pods watches the API and answers for every Service in the cluster. Because nearly every call starts with a lookup, those pods are a critical dependency: when they throttle or fail, everything reports that everything else is down.

cards.title: Headless Services return pod IPs
cards.body: A headless Service has no virtual IP; its DNS record returns the addresses of the backing pods directly. That is how stateful members find each other by name and how clients that pick their own endpoints, per-connection balancing or leader-aware routing, get the full list.

cards.title: Worked example: a name that resolves to nothing
cards.body: A pod calls api.payments and gets nowhere.
steps: Check the Service exists in the expected namespace
Check its selector matches the labels on the intended pods
List the Service’s endpoints; an empty list explains the timeouts
Fix the selector; the DNS name starts working because endpoints appear

cards.title: The ndots trap: five searches per name
cards.body: Pod resolvers are configured with a search list and ndots:5, so a short name is tried against each search domain before the name as written. One innocent-looking lookup of an external host can cost three or four queries, multiplied by every request the service makes.

cards.title: Trap: treating DNS as free
cards.body: Every lookup crosses the same small fleet of DNS pods, and search expansion multiplies the query count again. Bursty or misconfigured clients can saturate it. Node-local caches, fully-qualified names and watching DNS latency like any other dependency keep it invisible.

questions.prompt: From a pod in namespace shop, a lookup of the bare name api tries which name first?

choices.label: api.svc.cluster.local
api.shop.svc.cluster.local
api.cluster.local
api. as an absolute name

questions.explanation: The search list puts the pod’s own namespace first, so api expands to api.shop.svc.cluster.local before the cluster-level suffixes and finally the name as written.

questions.prompt: What does a headless Service’s DNS record return?

choices.label: A single virtual IP shared by its pods
The node IP running the first pod
The individual IPs of its ready pods
The ingress address of the cluster

questions.explanation: Headless means no virtual IP: DNS hands the caller the pod addresses so it can address members individually or balance itself. The other answers describe the normal ClusterIP path or things outside Service DNS entirely.

questions.prompt: A Service name resolves to an IP but every connection times out, and the Service’s selector matches no pods. What is the underlying gap?

choices.label: The DNS record’s TTL has expired
The name exists but there are no endpoints behind it
The pod’s resolver points outside the cluster
The virtual IP collides with another Service

questions.explanation: DNS resolved fine: the record exists because the Service exists. With a selector matching nothing, the endpoint list is empty, so the virtual IP has no pod to route to. Selector typos are the classic cause.

questions.prompt: A pod resolves 4,000 short names a second, and each expands through a 3-entry search list before the real lookup. How many queries a second reach cluster DNS?
assumptions: ndots:5 with a 3-entry search list
Each failed expansion is a full DNS query
questions.explanation: Design implication: one logical lookup became four DNS queries, so the DNS fleet carries several times the load the application team believes it sends; fully-qualified names remove the expansion.

questions.prompt: Order how a short name gets resolved inside a pod.

items.label: The name as written is tried last
The resolver counts the dots in the requested name
The answer comes back from the DNS pods
Each search-domain suffix is tried in turn

questions.explanation: With ndots above the name’s dot count the resolver works down the search list first and only then tries the name as written, so short names cost one extra query per suffix. A trailing dot marks the name absolute and skips the whole list.

questions.prompt: A latency-critical service makes hundreds of short calls a second to three internal names, and DNS adds jitter.
constraints: Pod IPs churn on every rollout

approaches.label: Resolve each pod IP once in the app and cache it forever
Use fully-qualified names or a node-local DNS cache to cut lookups
Hard-code the endpoint IPs into configuration

rationaleOptions.label: Hard-coded IPs remove DNS at no cost
Lookups still follow endpoint changes
Fewer expanded queries means less throttling
Caching pod IPs forever survives rollouts

rationaleConflicts.r3: Pods are replaced on every deploy; a stale IP is a dead call.
rationaleConflicts.r4: IPs churn with every scale event; the config rots immediately.

questions.explanation: The fix is fewer or closer lookups, not bypassing discovery: a trailing dot skips search expansion and a node-local cache shortens the path, while DNS still tracks the endpoints. Caching pod IPs or hard-coding them breaks silently the moment a rollout replaces the pods.

flashcards.back: No virtual IP; DNS returns the pods’ own IPs for direct addressing.
Names with fewer than five dots try the search domains before the name as written.

sources.title: Kubernetes: DNS for Services and Pods

mechanism.title: The life of a Service lookup
steps: Every pod is born with a resolv.conf written by the kubelet: the nameserver is the cluster DNS Service, the search list covers the pod’s own namespace first, and ndots defaults to five.

A bare name like api has fewer than five dots, so the resolver tries api.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local and the rest of the search list before the name as written; a trailing dot marks a name absolute and skips the expansion.
The DNS pods, a replicated deployment watching the API, answer with the Service’s records: a virtual IP for a normal Service, or the pod IPs themselves for a headless one.
For a normal Service the answer is one stable virtual IP; the node’s routing rules then translate connections to that IP onto one of the ready endpoint pods.
For a headless Service the answer is the set of pod IPs, which is how stateful members address each other by name and how clients that balance themselves get the live list.
Records follow the API with short TTLs, so endpoints appear and disappear with readiness; negative answers are cached too, which is why a just-created Service can briefly stay unknown.

Because every name in the cluster funnels through a small DNS fleet, it is sized, spread and sometimes cached per node like any other critical dependency, since an outage there looks like every service failing at once.

useWhen: Use normal Services for balanced access to interchangeable pods.
Use headless Services when clients must address members individually.
Fully qualify hot external names, or cache locally, to cut query amplification.
avoidWhen: Do not cache resolved pod IPs in the application; they churn with every rollout.
Avoid ignoring DNS in dependency maps; its overload fails everything at once.
Do not expect instant propagation; TTLs and negative caching add lag.

rows: One stable address, balanced for free
Client must handle the full IP list
Stale IPs break on every deploy

numbers.title: What ndots expansion does to DNS load
assumptions: A service resolves 4,000 short names a second (illustrative)
ndots:5 with a 3-entry search list expands each into four queries
A DNS pod comfortably serves about 8,000 queries a second
steps: Each logical lookup tries three search-suffixed names, then the real one: four queries.
4,000 × 4 = 16,000 queries a second lands on the DNS pods instead of 4,000.
At about 8,000 per pod, the expansion turns one DNS pod at half load into two at saturation.
Fully-qualifying the names returns the load to one query per lookup.
numbers.result: A resolver default quietly multiplies DNS load; bound it with FQDNs or a lower ndots.

india.title: The Kubernetes DNS specification
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation on DNS for Services and Pods defines the record layout: services get A or AAAA records under <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, headless services resolve to their backing pods, and pods receive a resolver configuration and DNS policy from the kubelet. The same documentation describes the ndots and search-list behaviour that turns one short name into several queries.

pitfalls.trap: “We resolved the pod IP once; we can keep using it.”
pitfalls.say: “Pod IPs die with the pod; re-resolve, or better, go through the Service.”

pitfalls.trap: “DNS is internal plumbing; it cannot be the bottleneck.”
pitfalls.say: “Every call in the cluster crosses a handful of DNS pods, and ndots expansion multiplies it further.”

takeaways: Service names resolve to a stable virtual IP or, headless, to pod IPs.
resolv.conf’s ndots and search list multiply queries on short names.
Never cache pod IPs; re-resolve or use the Service.
Cluster DNS is a critical dependency; size and cache it like one.

interactive.title: The trailing dot
interactive.prompt: A service calls partner.example.com thousands of times a minute. An engineer changes the configured name to partner.example.com. with a trailing dot. What changes?

choices.label: Each lookup skips the search list: one query instead of several
choices.feedback: Right: the dot marks the name absolute, so ndots expansion never runs.

choices.label: Nothing: the resolver ignores the trailing dot
choices.feedback: The dot is significant; it is what makes the name fully qualified.

choices.label: The lookups now bypass cluster DNS entirely
choices.feedback: The same resolver still answers; it just skips the search-suffix attempts.

interactive.reveal: On a hot name the trailing dot cuts DNS queries by the size of the search list. It is a one-character fix for a multiplied load.

seeAlso.why: DNS resolution, TTLs and negative caching are the same machinery at internet scale
Service discovery is the general pattern cluster DNS implements
Services and endpoints are what these DNS records describe

title: Database Change Management: Safe Migrations in the Pipeline
objectives: Explain why a schema must stay compatible with old and new code at once
Apply the expand-contract pattern to a destructive-looking change
Run migrations as a controlled pipeline step, not an application side effect

cards.title: Code rolls back; data does not
cards.body: Reverting a release puts old code back in minutes, but a destructive schema change has already moved or removed data. So every schema version must work with the code before and after it: the database lives in the overlap between releases, not inside either one.

cards.title: Expand, migrate, contract
cards.body: The safe pattern for a destructive-looking change: expand by adding the new shape alongside the old, migrate code and data onto it, then contract by removing the old shape once nothing released can still touch it. Three releases where one felt natural.

cards.title: Worked example: renaming a column without downtime
cards.body: A column used by live traffic needs a better name.
steps: Add the new column next to the old one
Deploy code that writes to both
Backfill existing rows in small batches
Deploy code that reads only the new column
Drop the old column in a later release

cards.title: Migrations run as a controlled step
cards.body: Migrations belong in the pipeline as one versioned step with a lock, timeouts and a record of what applied, ahead of the rollout it supports. That gives a single point to review, rehearse and retry, instead of whichever replica happens to boot first.

cards.title: Misconception: auto-migrate on startup is production-safe
cards.body: It works on one instance in staging. In production five replicas boot together and race the same change, a long statement locks a real table mid-traffic, and a half-applied failure leaves no release to roll back to. Boot is the worst place to learn a migration is slow.

cards.title: Trap: a migration that locks the table during the rollout
cards.body: Some engines still rewrite a table for innocent-looking changes, holding an exclusive lock while they do. On a large table that is minutes of stalled writes inside a deploy. Rehearse on a production-sized copy, set lock timeouts and batch the heavy work.

questions.prompt: During a rolling deploy, what must every intermediate schema version tolerate?

choices.label: Only queries from the newest release
Writes paused for the whole deploy
A separate schema per application version
Old and new code reading and writing it at once

questions.explanation: A rolling deploy runs both versions against the same schema for its duration, and a rollback extends that overlap backwards. Schemas that serve only one code version turn every deploy into a coordinated outage.

questions.prompt: Why is the old column dropped in a later release rather than the same one that stops reading it?

choices.label: A rollback then still finds the column it expects
Dropping columns always takes several days
Storage billing only updates monthly
The query planner keeps using the old name

questions.explanation: While a rollback of the reading release is possible, the old column is still live equipment. Drop it once nothing that could run again needs it; drops are fast, so the delay is about compatibility, not mechanics.

questions.prompt: Five app replicas each run pending schema migrations at boot. What is the failure mode?

choices.label: The migrations finish five times faster
Only the first replica can read the schema
Concurrent changes race, deadlock or apply partially
Migrations are idempotent, so extra runs cost nothing

questions.explanation: Schema changes are not safely parallel: replicas can interleave statements, deadlock on catalogue locks or die half-applied. Even when the tooling takes a lock, app boot gives it no review, timeout or retry discipline.

questions.prompt: A backfill must touch 12,000,000 rows. To keep replication lag low it writes batches of 20,000 rows every 5 seconds. About how long does it take?
assumptions: Batches are evenly sized and run back to back
The 5-second spacing is the pacing that keeps lag low
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 12 million rows at 4,000 rows a second is 3,000 seconds. An unbatched write could finish faster but would trade the wall-clock for lag spikes and lock contention during a live deploy.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a rehearsed schema change around a rolling deploy.

items.label: Run the single migration job ahead of the rollout
Ship a later release that contracts the old shape
Rehearse the migration on a production-sized copy
Roll out code that works with both shapes

questions.explanation: Rehearsal measures the lock time before it happens live, the single runner applies the change before any new code needs it, the rollout then straddles both shapes safely, and contraction waits until no released code can still touch the old shape.

questions.prompt: A 400 GB table needs a new column; deploys roll during the day and no maintenance window exists.
constraints: Deploys run old and new code together

approaches.label: Take the table offline overnight to run it
One ALTER in the deploy migration
Add the column, dual-write, backfill in batches, contract later

rationaleOptions.label: Each step keeps both code versions working
A single ALTER is quick on large tables
Batched writes avoid one giant lock
Scheduled downtime is simpler than batching

rationaleConflicts.r3: On a 400 GB table, some engines rewrite the whole thing under an exclusive lock.
rationaleConflicts.r4: There is no maintenance window, so offline is not on the table.

questions.explanation: Expand-contract trades one blocking moment for several boring steps, each compatible with whatever code is running. The single ALTER risks minutes of stalled writes, and the offline plan violates the no-window constraint outright.

flashcards.back: Add the new shape, migrate writes and data, then remove the old shape in a later release.

flashcards.front: Why not migrate at app boot?
flashcards.back: Replicas race the change, there is no review or timeout, and a half-applied failure has no clean rollback.

flashcards.front: Why drop the old column later?
flashcards.back: So a rollback of the reading release still finds the schema it expects.

mechanism.title: What a safe migration pipeline does
steps: Migrations are versioned, forward-only changes applied by a single runner in the pipeline, not by every app instance at boot; a lock or version table makes who applies unambiguous.
Each change is designed backward-compatible: the schema after the step must serve the code before and after the deploy, because a rolling deploy runs both at once.
For a destructive-looking change the runner expands instead: add the new shape, deploy code that writes to both, then backfill in measured batches while watching replication lag.
Reads switch only after the backfill completes and a deploy puts the reading code live; the old shape stays in place until no released version can still touch it.
The contract step, dropping the column or table, ships as its own later migration once rollback of the reading release is no longer needed.

Risky statements get guardrails: lock and statement timeouts, batching, online-change options where the engine offers them, and a rehearsal on a production-sized copy so lock time is measured rather than discovered.
Rollback means roll forward: because data has already moved, the undo path is a new compatible change, which is why each step is kept small and reversible by a forward fix.

useWhen: Expand-contract for any change on tables that serve live traffic.
One pipeline migration job ahead of the rollout, never per-replica at boot.
Batch backfills with lag monitoring on large tables.
avoidWhen: Do not auto-migrate from application startup in production.
Avoid whole-table rewrites during a deploy on engines that still do them.
Do not ship destructive changes in the same release that starts depending on them.

rows: May lock the table for the duration

numbers.title: The cost of one table rewrite
assumptions: A 400 GB table; the engine rewrites it under an exclusive lock (illustrative)
Sustained rewrite at 200 MB/s; batched online backfill at 4,000 rows a second
steps: Rewrite under lock: 400 GB ÷ 200 MB/s ≈ 2,000 s ≈ 33 minutes of stalled writes.
Through those minutes every write queues behind the lock, and user-facing timeouts start long before it ends.
A batched backfill over 12,000,000 rows at 20,000 rows per 5 s finishes in about 50 minutes with lag under a second.
Expand-contract trades a longer wall-clock for no single blocking moment.
numbers.result: On big tables the question is not how fast the change runs but how long it stops the world.

india.title: What PostgreSQL documents about locking
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: PostgreSQL’s ALTER TABLE documentation states that most forms of the command take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, blocking reads and writes for the duration, while some operations, such as adding a column with a non-volatile default since version 11, are optimised to avoid a full table rewrite. Those notes are why pipeline migrations set lock timeouts, rehearse on realistic data and batch large changes instead of running one heavyweight statement at deploy time.

pitfalls.trap: “Reverting the release commit undoes the migration.”
pitfalls.say: “A revert moves code back; the copied data and the dropped column do not come back with it.”
“On one instance in staging; in production several replicas race it against real data.”

takeaways: The schema must serve old and new code during every deploy.
Expand, dual-write, backfill, switch, then contract later.
One migration runner in the pipeline, never per-replica at boot.
Roll forward is the rollback plan for data.

interactive.title: The deploy-time lock
interactive.prompt: A pipeline runs a migration that adds a column to a 300 GB table; on this engine the statement rewrites the table under an exclusive lock. The rollout starts at the same moment. What do users see?

choices.label: Writes queue behind the lock for many minutes, surfacing as timeouts
choices.feedback: Right: the rewrite holds the lock until it finishes, and the lock is on the table itself.

choices.label: Nothing: adding a column is instant on any table
choices.feedback: On engines that rewrite the table, the duration scales with table size.

choices.label: A brief pause on one replica while the others serve
choices.feedback: The lock covers the table, not a replica, so every write waits.

interactive.reveal: Know which statements rewrite in your engine, set lock timeouts and rehearse on real data. For large tables, expand-contract with batched writes keeps the deploy boring.

seeAlso.why: Expand-contract is progressive delivery applied to the schema
Rolling deploys are what force backward-compatible schemas
Replication lag is the metric that paces a backfill
